title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale

paper.title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale
paper.abstract:
Abstract Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer.
However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored.
In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes.
We first introduce BlockSearch , a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 × 10\times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation.
We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention.
With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 × 7\times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 × 3\times higher score.
Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Retrieval—identifying the relevant document(s) in a corpus { D 1 , … , D N } \{D_{1},\dots,D_{N}\} for a query Q Q —has long been dominated by vector-based methods Karpukhin et al. (2020) . Recent advances in language modeling (LMs) suggest a more radical alternative: casting retrieval as conditional generation, where the model directly decodes the identifier of the relevant document from the corpus in-context ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Such in-context retrieval (ICR) could collapse retrieval and generation into a single model, replacing the two-stage retrieval-augmented generation pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) and enabling complex retrieval behavior beyond inner-product similarity ( Weller et al., 2025 ) . In other words, rather than relying on external harnesses (retrievers), the model itself decides which parts of its context are relevant to the task at hand. However, this possibility remains largely untested at realistic scale: prior work either relies on proprietary systems without controlled evaluation ( Lee et al., 2024 ) or studies reranking over small candidate sets ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) , rather than true corpus-scale retrieval. As a result, it remains unclear whether LMs can reliably retrieve relevant documents from large in-context corpora ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) . ICR differs fundamentally from standard long-context modeling. Rather than processing a single coherent sequence, it operates over large collections of independent documents, creating both opportunities and challenges. On one hand, document-level independence naturally enables parallel encoding and caching. On the other hand, effective retrieval requires two capabilities that current LMs struggle with: (C1) scaling to corpora containing millions of tokens, and (C2) generalizing to corpus sizes far beyond those seen during training. Both are difficult in practice: million-token attention remains computationally expensive, while extrapolation to substantially longer contexts is known to be brittle in modern LMs ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Nakanishi, 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) . To this end, we present the first systematic study of whether an LM can act as a corpus-scale retriever under these conditions. We first introduce BlockSearch ( § 3 ), a 0.6B-parameter LM retriever that builds on prior ICR architectures using block-sparse attention ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) . For scale and length generalization, it adds randomized per-document identifier codes, in-batch negative training, and an on-policy auxiliary loss that trains on the model’s own rolled-out digit prefixes. On widely studied retrieval benchmarks (e.g., MS MARCO and NQ), BlockSearch matches a dense retriever at smaller corpus sizes ( 95.8 % 95.8\% vs. 95.5 % 95.5\% on MS MARCO at ∼ \sim 45k tokens), and maintains non-trivial accuracy beyond the LM baseline, generalizing up to 10 × 10\times beyond its training context. Despite these improvements, BlockSearch still collapses at large scale: recall approaches zero near million-token contexts, remaining far below a simple dense retrieval baseline. We trace this failure not to a ranking collapse, but to an attention dilution effect, a degradation that has also been observed in other settings ( Nakanishi, 2025 ; Veličković et al., 2024 ; Barbero et al., 2024 ; Duvvuri et al., 2026 ) . Leveraging the natural alignment between queries and their gold documents, we find that the transformer usually assigns the highest pre-softmax attention score to the gold document even at million-token scale, but the aggregate contribution of irrelevant documents to the softmax denominator grows faster with corpus size, causing the normalized attention mass on the gold document to collapse ( § 4 ). Motivated by this analysis, we consider two techniques to mitigate attention dilution at extreme context lengths (§ 5 ). First, length-aware sinks reshape the effective softmax denominator, reducing the influence of diffuse attention without modifying QK scores. Second, document-level sparse attention reduces the number of documents participating in attention at intermediate layers ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Ohayon et al., 2025 ) . Together, these methods mitigate the effects of attention dilution. On well-studied retrieval benchmarks (e.g. MSMARCO and NQ from BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) ), they improve million-token Recall@1 from as little as 0.2 % 0.2\% to 20.5 % 20.5\% , recovering the gap to dense retrieval. They also match or exceed MSA ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , a concurrent LM trained on much longer contexts with 7 × 7\times more parameters. On benchmarks requiring more complex notions of similarity, where dense retrieval tends to fail, such as LIMIT ( Weller et al., 2025 ) , our method exceeds Qwen3-dense by nearly 3 × 3\times ( § 6 ). Our results establish corpus-scale in-context retrieval as a viable alternative to dense retrieval under both scale and length extrapolation. More broadly, they identify attention dilution as the primary bottleneck at million-token scale: while simple interventions can substantially mitigate its effects, it remains a fundamental challenge for scalable in-context retrieval.

sections.heading: In-context and generative retrieval.
sections.text: Most long-context evaluation work focuses on synthetic retrieval-style tasks such as Needle-in-a-Haystack and RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) , potentially overstating real-world retrieval capability. The premise that an LM can subsume dense retrieval is first articulated by Lee et al. (2024) , primarily evaluating proprietary Gemini systems. Subsequent work studies LMs as rerankers over small candidate pools using block-sparse attention and relevance heads in intermediate Transformer layers ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, we study LMs as corpus-scale retrievers, training with small contexts and evaluating up to 10 4 10^{4} documents ( ∼ \sim 1M tokens) in an effort to elicit length-generalization. Generative retrieval ( Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ) also decodes with identifiers, but stores corpus information in model parameters, requiring retraining when the corpus changes. In contrast, ICR encodes the corpus explicitly in context, allowing corpus updates without retraining.

sections.heading: Sparse and routed attention.
sections.text: A large body of work makes long-context attention tractable by routing or sparsification; our document-level sparse attention proposed in § 4 builds on this line of work. Prior approaches reduce attention cost through inference-time pruning ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , block-sparse kernels ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ) , learned block routing ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) , or hierarchical sparse attention ( Leng et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . Our work is grounded in this literature, but the retrieval setting introduces unique opportunities and challenges. The most directly comparable work is concurrent: MSA-4B ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which, like BlockSearch , learns to perform generative document citation from an in-context corpus. However, the two works focus on different questions: MSA primarily scales the retrieval recipe through larger models and extensive training, whereas our work studies the fundamental failure modes of ICR as corpus size grows. In fact, our proposed methods targeting these failure modes match or exceed MSA despite using 7 × 7\times fewer parameters and significantly shorter training-time contexts (§ 5 ).

sections.heading: Attention sinks and softmax dilution.
sections.text: Streaming-LLM ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) introduces explicit attention sinks for stable long-context decoding, and the gpt-oss model card ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) documents a null-attention mechanism that absorbs unused softmax mass. Whereas these works use sinks for streaming stability, we apply them to mitigate softmax dilution under large N N . A number of results show that as the number of attended tokens grows, the softmax distribution flattens, removing attention peaks ( Nakanishi, 2025 ; Veličković et al., 2024 ; Duvvuri et al., 2026 ) ; this loss of sensitivity has been tied to representational collapse in longer contexts ( Barbero et al., 2024 ; Jacob et al., 2024 ) . We show that the primary cause of retrieval degradation with growing context is softmax dilution, and that softmax-adjusting mechanisms such as sinks may hold the key to mitigating its effects.

sections.heading: 3 BlockSearch : Model and Million-Token Evaluation
sections.text: We first investigate several training-time improvements to the standard long-context retrieval recipe. After reviewing the problem setup ( § 3.1 ), we describe the changes that constitute BlockSearch ( § 3.2 ), our evaluation setup ( § 3.3 ), and the results ( § 3.4 ). These results motivate the later analysis of possible failure modes ( § 4 ) and promising lines for even further improvements ( § 5 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Setup
sections.text: Given a corpus of N N documents and a query, the model must generate the identifier of the document that best answers the query. The corpus is tokenized with at most T doc = 300 T_{\text{doc}}{=}300 tokens per document and prefilled into the KV cache; the query is appended, and the model autoregressively decodes a four-digit code in { 0 , … , 9999 } \{0,\dots,9999\} that maps back to one document (that’s hopefully relevant). This concretizes challenges C1 and C2 from § 1 : just 10,000 documents at ∼ \sim 100 tokens each well exceeds the 32K-token native context of the Qwen3-0.6B backbone, and the model must generalize to corpora substantially larger than those seen during training: again, a requirement that distinguishes retrievers from rerankers and has been largely overlooked in prior LM-retrieval work.

sections.heading: 3.2 Method: BlockSearch
sections.text: We now describe BlockSearch : whenever possible, we follow prior ICR work, but our requirements C1 and C2 expose several limitations that motivate our proposed improvements.

sections.heading: Prompt format.
sections.text: Prior in-context work assigns each document a sequential integer identifier from 1 1 to N N ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . In our regime, training-time IDs are a strict subset of inference IDs and risk overfitting to absolute position. We instead insert each document as <bos>Doc {code}: {text} (Doc {code})<eos> , with {code} drawn uniformly at random per training step, breaking any association between code, semantics, or position. We also drop the query prefix from prior work ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) : while it improves performance, it prevents corpus reuse across queries, which is cost-prohibitive at our scale. For a full example of a corpus/query prompt, we refer the reader to appendix A .

sections.heading: Block-sparse attention.
sections.text: Causal prefill scales quadratically in tokens, which is prohibitive at our target N N . Since documents are disjoint, we use a block-sparse mask ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) : document tokens attend causally only within their own block, and the query block attends over the full corpus and causally to itself. Following common practice ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) , we reset RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) positions at each document start and shift the query to position 300. The mask is materialized via flex_attention ( Dong et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: We train on the ReLabeled Hard Negatives (RLHN) version of BEIR ( Thakur et al., 2025 ) , which uses an LLM judge to prune false negatives from mined hard negatives in datasets such as MS MARCO ( Bajaj et al., 2016 ) . Per query we keep one pruned positive and 15 hard negatives; per-query relevance scores for the auxiliary loss are from Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . The training corpus totals ∼ \sim 100M tokens; full mix and cleaning details are in appendix C .

sections.heading: Training regime.
sections.text: Inspired by in-batch contrastive training ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Qu et al., 2021 ) , we adapt in-batch negatives to this setting. For a batch of b b (query, 16-document) tuples (1 positive + 15 hard negatives each), we prefill all b × 16 b{\times}16 documents once (re-randomizing codes) and score every query against the shared corpus, converting one prefill into b b training signals. Every model is trained with 256 documents in its corpus, i.e. b = 16 b{=}16 .

sections.heading: Training objective.
sections.text: We train with teacher forcing on the gold code, but this alon causes an exposure bias issue: at inference, each digit conditions on the model’s own potentially incorrect prefix, which lies off the training distribution. We therefore add an on-policy auxiliary loss. The model first rolls out a four-digit code from its own distribution with gradients disabled. For each digit position, we construct a teacher distribution from in-batch document scores, restricted to candidates whose prefix matches the rollout. We then replay the rollout with gradients enabled at the four answer positions and average the resulting cross-entropy losses. The total loss is ℒ = ℒ CE + λ ​ ℒ aux \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}} with λ \lambda ramped in after a warmup; the full algorithm can be found in algorithm 1 ( appendix F ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Evaluation
sections.text: The model is judged by whether it can recover the relevant document from those placed in context; our metric is Recall@1 over the generated four-digit codes, decoded by a beam search over the digit sequence. We also evaluate Recall@5 using beam search over the top five predictions and observe trends consistent with Recall@1; see appendix J for details.

sections.heading: Evaluation data.
sections.text: We evaluate on three BEIR datasets ( Thakur et al., 2021 ) : MS MARCO (dev), HotpotQA (test), and NQ (test). We choose these datasets because they are among the most widely studied retrieval benchmarks, on which dense retrievers have been extensively optimized, providing a strong calibration point for comparison. We later complement these evaluations with benchmarks requiring different notions of similarity, where dense retrieval struggles (§ 6 ). For each dataset, we sample 400 queries without replacement from the its split. For each query, we take its gold document and 24 hard negatives (retrieved using Qwen3-Embedding-8B Zhang et al. (2025b) ); by taking a union of these documents across all 400 queries, we get a 10,000 document corpus. In contrast with prior work Lee et al. (2024) , the substantial use of hard negatives makes the input corpus far more challenging. 1 1 1 For NQ, we use fewer hard negatives per query due to longer documents; per-dataset sizes are in appendix B ( table 4 ). To evaluate across varying corpus sizes (e.g. N = 500 N{=}500 to N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 ), we also construct smaller versions of each dataset. We first include every query’s gold document (400 documents), then fill out the rest of the dataset with documents randomly selected from the full 10,000 document corpus.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against two reference retrievers and two ablations of BlockSearch itself: • BlockSearch -position : sequential codes ( 0 , … , 9999 0,\dots,9999 by document position) to isolate the contribution of random codes, and no auxiliary loss; this corresponds to the prior ICR recipe. • BlockSearch -offpolicy : BlockSearch with the on-policy auxiliary loss removed (teacher-forced CE only); isolates the exposure-bias fix. • Qwen3-dense (0.6B) : a dense retriever trained on the same RLHN data ( Thakur et al., 2025 ) with a contrastive objective ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) from the same Qwen3-0.6B backbone ( appendix E ); our primary reference point and the dense-retrieval gold standard BlockSearch must clear to be practical. • MSA-4B ( Chen et al., 2026 ) : a concurrent multi-million-token LM, ∼ \sim 7 × 7\times larger and trained with a much larger long-context budget, sidestepping the C2 generalization requirement; an oracle reference.

sections.heading: BlockSearch improves extrapolation in LMs, up to ~500,000 tokens.
sections.text: All LMs perform strongly at small N N ( > 95 % >95\% on MS MARCO at N = 1,000 N{=}1{,}000 ), but baselines degrade much faster. The position-coded variant, which is the prior ICR method, collapses to near-zero by N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 on every dataset. BlockSearch -offpolicy trails BlockSearch (MS MARCO 15.0 15.0 vs. 18.8 18.8 at N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 ; HotpotQA 6.2 6.2 vs. 13.0 13.0 ), showing that random codes and the on-policy loss contribute distinct gains. Note that, while BlockSearch substantially improves extrapolation, all variants eventually collapse beyond roughly 500,000 500{,}000 tokens, corresponding to about 10 × 10\times the training context length.

sections.heading: BlockSearch vs. MSA-4B.
sections.text: Despite having ∼ \sim 7 × 7\times fewer parameters than MSA ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , BlockSearch matches MSA at N = 500 , 1000 N{=}500,1000 and 2500 2500 , e.g., on MS MARCO, achieving 95.8 % , 75.2 % , 43.8 % 95.8\%,75.2\%,43.8\% vs. 93.8 % , 70.2 % , 42.2 % 93.8\%,70.2\%,42.2\% for MSA. At large corpus sizes, MSA-4B pulls ahead ( 27.5 % 27.5\% vs. 18.8 % 18.8\% at N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 , 16.0 % 16.0\% vs. 0.2 % 0.2\% at N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 ), which is expected given that MSA is explicitly trained for long-context tasks, whereas these settings require BlockSearch to generalize to corpora 20 20 – 40 × 40\times larger than those seen during training. Despite near-perfect long-context performance on synthetic evaluation such as RULER’s needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) as reported in the original paper ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , MSA degrades sharply on real retrieval tasks: substantially more than the dense retrieval baseline. This suggests that realistic retrieval settings are significantly more challenging than existing synthetic long-context benchmarks, highlighting the need for the long-context literature to adopt more semantically meaningful retrieval tasks in evaluation.

sections.heading: BlockSearch vs. dense retrieval.
sections.text: Dense retrieval also degrades with N N but without the sharp LM collapse: BlockSearch matches the Qwen3-dense gold standard at small and mid N N but trails it at large N N (MS MARCO 18.8 18.8 vs. 38.5 38.5 at N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 ; near-zero vs. 20.2 20.2 at N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 ), with similar trends on NQ and HotpotQA. Closing this large- N N gap remains the central challenge for practical in-context retrieval and motivates the mechanistic analysis in § 4 .

sections.heading: 4 Understanding the Large- N N Deterioration
sections.text: § 3 shows that BlockSearch generalizes well past its training-time context length, but still collapses at N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 . In this section, we posit that this collapse can be decomposed into two parts: a per-head, per-layer measure of attention recall (does the relevant document receive the highest attention score?) remains deep into the large- N N regime, while generation recall (does the model decode the correct identifier?) collapses. We also find that the share of each attention layer’s output that comes from gold tokens collapses while the layer’s overall output magnitude is largely preserved, cleanly encapsulating the aformentioned attention dilution issue.

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Decoder language models are not a homogeneous stack: layers and heads take on specific functional roles, with FFNs promoting concepts ( Geva et al., 2021 ; Geva et al., 2022 ) , induction heads carrying in-context learning ( Olsson et al., 2022 ) , and a sparse subset of retrieval heads carrying the long-context retrieval signal ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . For in-context retrieval specifically, BlockRank ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) , ICR 2 ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , and QRHeads ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) build on those results, observing that per-head attention scores can serve directly as a relevance signal. This observation is the starting point for the measurements we report.

sections.heading: Heads no longer agree on the gold document.

The retrieval band erodes under the sum aggregator: R 19 sum R^{\text{sum}}_{19} drops from 0.97 0.97 at N = 500 N{=}500 to 0.01 0.01 at N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 , matching the collapse in generation recall reported in § 3.4 . sections.text: The vector-level result of table 1 is driven by a single mechanism inside each head. As N N grows, gold’s largest pre-softmax score s L , t ⋆ h s^{h}_{L,t^{\star}} (with t ⋆ = arg ⁡ max t ∈ 𝒢 ⁡ s L , t h t^{\star}=\arg\max_{t\in\mathcal{G}}s^{h}_{L,t} ) no longer dominates over the larger pool of competing distractor scores, so the post-softmax weight assigned to gold’s value vector shrinks and the per-head readout u L h u^{h}_{L} becomes a non-gold average at comparable magnitude. This length-driven softmax dispersion is a generic phenomenon ( Nakanishi, 2025 ; Veličković et al., 2024 ; Barbero et al., 2024 ) and an empirical driver of length-generalization failure across tasks ( Li et al., 2025 ; Vasylenko et al., 2025 ) ; the contribution here is connecting it to a vector-level swap at the residual stream rather than treating it as an abstract probability-mass collapse. § 5 then evaluates two avenues of improvement that target this mechanism.

sections.heading: 5 Addressing the Attention Dilution Problem
sections.text: Having identified softmax dispersion under growing N N as the guilty party, we study two potential directions that address it. We first consider two length-aware modifications to attention softmax that mitigate the dispersion issue. We also consider document-level sparse attention , thereby pruning the set of tokens that enter the softmax.

sections.heading: Length-aware softmax.
sections.text: We first describe two methods that change how softmax converts the pre-softmax scores s L , t h s^{h}_{L,t} to attention weights. Both are length-aware : each carries a corpus-size signal that lets the softmax adapt to the large N N setting. An additive sink appends a learned constant to the softmax denominator, so a head whose largest scores fall below that constant leaks probability mass into the appended slot and emits a small attention output ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) ; the per-token weights α ~ L , t h \tilde{\alpha}^{h}_{L,t} no longer sum to one. The length-awareness is implicit: training under a wide range of effective corpus sizes N eff ∼ LogUniform ⁡ ( 128 , 5000 ) N_{\text{eff}}\sim\mathrm{LogUniform}(128,5000) ) lets the learned scalar absorb a length signal, so the gate fires more often at large N N where attention is diffuse. Multiplicative score rescaling keeps a proper softmax but sharpens it, and is length-aware by construction: SSMax ( Nakanishi, 2025 ) multiplies the pre-softmax scores by s ⋅ log ⁡ N s\cdot\log N (for a tuned scaling parameter s s ) so that the gap between the largest score and the bulk grows directly with N N . Following GPT-OSS ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) we instantiate the sink with a learned scalar b L ∈ ℝ b_{L}\in\mathbb{R} per attention layer: α ~ L , t h = exp ⁡ ( s L , t h ) ∑ t ′ exp ⁡ ( s L , t ′ h ) + exp ⁡ ( b L ) . \tilde{\alpha}^{h}_{L,t}\;=\;\frac{\exp(s^{h}_{L,t})}{\sum_{t^{\prime}}\exp(s^{h}_{L,t^{\prime}})+\exp(b_{L})}. (5) The appended slot has no value vector, so ∑ t α ~ L , t h ≤ 1 \sum_{t}\tilde{\alpha}^{h}_{L,t}\leq 1 and a layer with diffuse attention writes a smaller residual update (gate-form derivation in appendix H ). We refer to the resulting model as BlockSearch -sink. We then produce BlockSearch -SSMax following Nakanishi (2025) with s s initialized to 0.43 0.43 at every attention layer. Both models compose with the block-sparse attention pattern and train seamlessly with the changes in § 3 .

sections.heading: Document-level sparse attention.
sections.text: On the flip side, we also consider scoring documents and keeping a top- B B shortlist before the code generation is performed; this is a popular approach in long-context research that prunes the context down into a manageable state Chen et al. (2026) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Ohayon et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Hu et al. (2024) . We perform a doc-level routing step at L ​ 16 \mathrm{L}16 , immediately upstream of the retrieval band ( § 4.2 ): a forward pass through L ​ 0 \mathrm{L}0 – L ​ 15 \mathrm{L}15 produces the per-document score R 16 sum ​ ( d ) R^{\text{sum}}_{16}(d) from § 4.2 ; only the tokens of the top B = 256 B{=}256 documents participate in dense attention at L ​ 17 \mathrm{L}17 onward. We call this BlockSearch -routing, and we pick doc-level over token-level because each document is a conveniently coherent semantic unit. We refer the reader to appendix I for more information on the choice of B B .

sections.heading: 6 Out-of-Distribution Generalization: LIMIT
sections.text: Experiments in § 3 – § 5 focused on widely studied retrieval benchmarks that dense retrieval has been heavily optimized for. BlockSearch , with the proposed modifications, matches dense retrieval, which is a notable milestone given that these benchmarks largely define the strengths of dense retrieval. However, a fundamental question remains: can in-context retrieval actually outperform dense retrieval, going beyond matching it? To answer this question, we evaluate BlockSearch on LIMIT ( Weller et al., 2025 ) , a benchmark requiring a lexical notion of similarity, where dense retrieval struggles. Under a strict out-of-distribution evaluation setup, BlockSearch significantly outperforms dense retrieval. 2 2 2 For additional out-of-distribution results, we also provide figures for the OBLIQ evaluation ( Tchuindjo et al., 2026 ) in Appendix L .

sections.heading: Attention vs. readout.
sections.text: The attention ceiling R 19 any R^{\text{any}}_{19} stays at 1.00 1.00 across the entire sweep, from N = 46 N{=}46 up to N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 ( ∼ \sim 850k tokens): at every corpus size at least one head still ranks a gold document first. The gap between the two is the same readout bottleneck identified in § 4 , now both out of distribution (a lexical task that BlockSearch never trained on; its training mix is semantic, appendix C ) and length-generalized: the per-head retrieval signal persists while the code-generation readout cannot recover it.

sections.heading: Routing.
sections.text: Of our modifications, SSMax+routing performs the best, with R@1 at 0.149 0.149 at N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 while BlockSearch and BlockSearch -sink are at zero. SSMax also helps at mid- N N , but reaches 0.054 0.054 R@1 by N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 . The length-aware sink does not help on this lexical benchmark: BlockSearch -sink trails BlockSearch at every N N (e.g. 0.252 0.252 vs. 0.354 0.354 at N = 46 N{=}46 ), in contrast to its roughly neutral effect on MS MARCO. BlockSearch -SSMax-routing also stays above the same-backbone pooled Qwen3-dense retriever at every N N ( 0.149 0.149 vs. 0.035 0.035 at N = 5,000 N{=}5{,}000 ), suggesting that our methods do offer better out-of-distribution performance and potential extension to more complex tasks beyond basic semantic search.

sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: Routing delays but does not prevent the inevitable: BlockSearch -SSMax-routing is still declining with N N ( 0.149 0.149 at ∼ \sim 850k tokens). Thus, these modifications extend functional LIMIT retrieval to larger corpora, rather than solving it, which remains an open problem.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we presented the first systematic study of corpus-scale in-context retrieval with long-context language models, focusing on two requirements expected of practical retrieval systems: scaling to million-token corpora and generalizing to corpus sizes far beyond those seen during training. We showed that, with appropriate training and architectural modifications, LMs can perform meaningful retrieval far beyond their nominal training regime, approaching dense retrieval performance at moderate scales. The story is a tale of two cities: on benchmarks built around single-vector retrieval, our methods match a strong dense baseline at million-token scale, while on LIMIT, designed to defeat embedding similarity, they exceed it by nearly 3 × 3\times . At the same time, we identified attention dispersion as a fundamental scaling bottleneck: even when retrieval signals remain internally present, normalized attention mass collapses under extreme context growth. Motivated by this analysis, we demonstrated that length-aware tweaks to attention substantially improve retrieval performance at million-token scale. Together, our results suggest that scalable in-context retrieval is both promising and fundamentally constrained by attention dilution, motivating new directions for retrieval architectures and long-context modeling.

sections.heading: Appendix A Prompt Format
sections.text: To make the input format used by BlockSearch concrete, fig. 4 shows a worked example for a single MS MARCO query against a four-document corpus. Each document is wrapped between BOS/EOS markers and bracketed by its randomly-assigned four-digit code ( § 3.2 ); RoPE [ 30 ] positions are reset to 0 0 at every BOS so that the document tokens occupy positions 0 0 – T doc T_{\text{doc}} regardless of where the document sits in the prefill. Document tokens attend causally only inside their own block. After the corpus, the query block is appended at RoPE position T doc = 300 T_{\text{doc}}{=}300 and attends to the entire prefilled corpus. The query block carries an instruction prefix, the query, and the four answer slots; the model is supervised to emit the four-digit code identifying the gold document and is decoded autoregressively at inference. The same template is used at training and at evaluation, with one difference: at training time the four answer digits are teacher-forced and the on-policy auxiliary loss ( appendix F ) replays the model’s own rollout at the same four positions. # Document blocks: one per corpus document, codes sampled uniformly per training step. sections.text: § 3.2 introduces an on-policy auxiliary loss to mitigate exposure bias when decoding the four-digit code. The procedure is given in algorithm 1 . For each query in the batch, we have K K candidate documents (1 positive, 15 hard negatives) with their full four-digit codes and Qwen3-Embedding-8B relevance scores, and the corpus has already been prefilled into the shared block-sparse cache ( § 3.2 ). Sample a code a ^ = a ^ 1 ​ … ​ a ^ L \hat{a}=\hat{a}_{1}\dots\hat{a}_{L} autoregressively from π θ \pi_{\theta} with gradients off. 5: 6: (2) Build a per-position teacher. For each digit position t t : 7: Keep candidates whose first t − 1 t-1 digits match the rollout: ℳ t = { k : c < t ( k ) = a ^ < t } \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{k:c^{(k)}_{<t}=\hat{a}_{<t}\} . 8: Set the teacher distribution over the 10 10 digits to the candidate-weighted vote: q t ( d ) ∝ ∑ k ∈ ℳ t w k ⋅ 𝟙 [ c t ( k ) = d ] . q_{t}(d)\;\propto\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}w_{k}\cdot\mathds{1}[c^{(k)}_{t}=d]. 9: 10: (3) Replay with gradients. Re-decode the four answer positions conditioned on a ^ < t \hat{a}_{<t} (the rollout’s prefix, not the gold prefix) with gradients on, obtaining the student distributions π θ ( ⋅ ∣ a ^ < t ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\hat{a}_{<t}) . 11: 12: Loss: ℒ aux = 1 L ∑ t = 1 L CE ( q t , π θ ( ⋅ ∣ a ^ < t ) ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}=\dfrac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathrm{CE}\!\bigl(q_{t},\;\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\hat{a}_{<t})\bigr) , added to the total loss as ℒ = ℒ CE + λ ​ ℒ aux \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} . The rollout uses the model’s own distribution rather than the gold code, so the prefixes that the four answer positions condition on are exactly the prefixes the model would visit at inference. The per-position teacher q t q_{t} thus plays the role of a DAgger expert [ 47 ] : at every state visited along the model’s own trajectory, it specifies what the model should have done. Then for every t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , α ~ L , t h = α L , t h ⋅ g L h . \tilde{\alpha}^{h}_{L,t}\;=\;\alpha^{h}_{L,t}\cdot g^{h}_{L}. Proof. sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: The gate g L h ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) g^{h}_{L}\in(0,1) depends only on the per-(layer, head) comparison between lse ⁡ ( s ) \mathrm{lse}(s) — a measure of how much pre-softmax mass the layer’s logits already concentrate — and the learned threshold b L b_{L} . When the layer’s logits are sharp and concentrated relative to b L b_{L} (large lse \mathrm{lse} ), g L h → 1 g^{h}_{L}\to 1 and eq. 5 reduces to the standard softmax. When the logits are diffuse and many tokens contribute small amounts (small lse \mathrm{lse} relative to b L b_{L} ), g L h → 0 g^{h}_{L}\to 0 and the layer’s contribution to the residual update a L a_{L} is suppressed multiplicatively. This is the mechanism by which the sink “costs” a noisy layer its write to the residual stream without altering the relative ranking of the per-token weights.

sections.heading: Appendix I Top- B B Routing Recall
sections.text: The top- B B routing of § 5 hinges on the assumption that the router can keep the gold document inside a small top- B B shortlist with high probability across our checkpoints. Math and Writing are analogues tasks: the query is a passage (a competition mathematics problem, or a paragraph of prose), and the gold documents are other passages that share an abstract reasoning pattern or argument with it despite entirely different surface content. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.01538v1 [cs.CL] 01 Jul 2026 Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale Siddharth Gollapudi † † thanks: Correspondence to sgollapu@berkeley.edu . Affiliation: UC Berkeley Nilesh Gupta Affiliation: UT Austin Prasann Singhal Affiliation: UC Berkeley Sewon Min Affiliation: UC Berkeley Abstract Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch , a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 × 10\times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 × 7\times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 × 3\times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge. 1 Introduction Retrieval—identifying the relevant document(s) in a corpus { D 1 , … , D N } \{D_{1},\dots,D_{N}\} for a query Q Q —has long been dominated by vector-based methods Karpukhin et al. (2020) . Recent advances in language modeling (LMs) suggest a more radical alternative: casting retrieval as conditional generation, where the model directly decodes the identifier of the relevant document from the corpus in-context ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Such in-context retrieval (ICR) could collapse retrieval and generation into a single model, replacing the two-stage retrieval-augmented generation pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) and enabling complex retrieval behavior beyond inner-product similarity ( Weller et al., 2025 ) . In other words, rather than relying on external harnesses (retrievers), the model itself decides which parts of its context are relevant to the task at hand. However, this possibility remains largely untested at realistic scale: prior work either relies on proprietary systems without controlled evaluation ( Lee et al., 2024 ) or studies reranking over small candidate sets ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) , rather than true corpus-scale retrieval. As a result, it remains unclear whether LMs can reliably retrieve relevant documents from large in-context corpora ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) . ICR differs fundamentally from standard long-context modeling. Rather than processing a single coherent sequence, it operates over large collections of independent documents, creating both opportunities and challenges. On one hand, document-level independence naturally enables parallel encoding and caching. On the other hand, effective retrieval requires two capabilities that current LMs struggle with: (C1) scaling to corpora containing millions of tokens, and (C2) generalizing to corpus sizes far beyond those seen during training. Both are difficult in practice: million-token attention remains computationally expensive, while extrapolation to substantially longer contexts is known to be brittle in modern LMs ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Nakanishi, 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) . To this end, we present the first systematic study of whether an LM can act as a corpus-scale retriever under these conditions. We first introduce BlockSearch ( § 3 ), a 0.6B-parameter LM retriever that builds on prior ICR architectures using block-sparse attention ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) . For scale and length generalization, it adds randomized per-document identifier codes, in-batch negative training, and an on-policy auxiliary loss that trains on the model’s own rolled-out digit prefixes. On widely studied retrieval benchmarks (e.g., MS MARCO and NQ), BlockSearch matches a dense retriever at smaller corpus sizes ( 95.8 % 95.8\% vs. 95.5 % 95.5\% on MS MARCO at ∼ \sim 45k tokens), and maintains non-trivial accuracy beyond the LM baseline, generalizing up to 10 × 10\times beyond its training context. Despite these improvements, BlockSearch still collapses at large scale: recall approaches zero near million-token contexts, remaining far below a simple dense retrieval baseline. We trace this failure not to a ranking collapse, but to an attention dilution effect, a degradation that has also been observed in other settings ( Nakanishi, 2025 ; Veličković et al., 2024 ; Barbero et al., 2024 ; Duvvuri et al., 2026 ) . Leveraging the natural alignment between queries and their gold documents, we find that the transformer usually assigns the highest pre-softmax attention score to the gold document even at million-token scale, but the aggregate contribution of irrelevant documents to the softmax denominator grows faster with corpus size, causing the normalized attention mass on the gold document to collapse ( § 4 ). Motivated by this analysis, we consider two techniques to mitigate attention dilution at extreme context lengths (§ 5 ). First, length-aware sinks reshape the effective softmax denominator, reducing the influence of diffuse attention without modifying QK scores. Second, document-level sparse attention reduces the number of documents participating in attention at intermediate layers ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Ohayon et al., 2025 ) . Together, these methods mitigate the effects of attention dilution. On well-studied retrieval benchmarks (e.g. MSMARCO and NQ from BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) ), they improve million-token Recall@1 from as little as 0.2 % 0.2\% to 20.5 % 20.5\% , recovering the gap to dense retrieval. They also match or exceed MSA ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , a concurrent LM trained on much longer contexts with 7 × 7\times more parameters. On benchmarks requiring more complex notions of similarity, where dense retrieval tends to fail, such as LIMIT ( Weller et al., 2025 ) , our method exceeds Qwen3-dense by nearly 3 × 3\times ( § 6 ). Our results establish corpus-scale in-context retrieval as a viable alternative to dense retrieval under both scale and length extrapolation. More broadly, they identify attention dilution as the primary bottleneck at million-token scale: while simple interventions can substantially mitigate its effects, it remains a fundamental challenge for scalable in-context retrieval. 2 Related Work In-context and generative retrieval. Most long-context evaluation work focuses on synthetic retrieval-style tasks such as Needle-in-a-Haystack and RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) , potentially overstating real-world retrieval capability. The premise that an LM can subsume dense retrieval is first articulated by Lee et al. (2024) , primarily evaluating proprietary Gemini systems. Subsequent work studies LMs as rerankers over small candidate pools using block-sparse attention and relevance heads in intermediate Transformer layers ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, we study LMs as corpus-scale retrievers, training with small contexts and evaluating up to 10 4 10^{4} documents ( ∼ \sim 1M tokens) in an effort to elicit length-generalization. Generative retrieval ( Tay et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ) also decodes with identifiers, but stores corpus information in model parameters, requiring retraining when the corpus changes. In contrast, ICR encodes the corpus explicitly in context, allowing corpus updates without retraining. Sparse and routed attention. A large body of work makes long-context attention tractable by routing or sparsification; our document-level sparse attention proposed in § 4 builds on this line of work. Prior approaches reduce attention cost through inference-time pruning ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , block-sparse kernels ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ) , learned block routing ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) , or hierarchical sparse attention ( Leng et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . Our work is grounded in this literature, but the retrieval setting introduces unique opportunities and challenges. The most directly comparable work is concurrent: MSA-4B ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which, like BlockSearch , learns to perform generative document citation from an in-context corpus. However, the two works focus on different questions: MSA primarily scales the retrieval recipe through larger models and extensive training, whereas our work studies the fundamental failure modes of ICR as corpus size grows. In fact, our proposed methods targeting these failure modes match or exceed MSA despite using 7 × 7\times fewer parameters and significantly shorter training-time contexts (§ 5 ). Attention sinks and softmax dilution. Streaming-LLM ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) introduces explicit attention sinks for stable long-context decoding, and the gpt-oss model card ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) documents a null-attention mechanism that absorbs unused softmax mass. Whereas these works use sinks for streaming stability, we apply them to mitigate softmax dilution under large N N . A number of results show that as the number of attended tokens grows, the softmax distribution flattens, removing attention peaks ( Nakanishi, 2025 ; Veličković et al., 2024 ; Duvvuri et al., 2026 ) ; this loss of sensitivity has been tied to representational collapse in longer contexts ( Barbero et al., 2024 ; Jacob et al., 2024 ) . We show that the primary cause of retrieval degradation with growing context is softmax dilution, and that softmax-adjusting mechanisms such as sinks may hold the key to mitigating its effects. 3 BlockSearch : Model and Million-Token Evaluation We first investigate several training-time improvements to the standard long-context retrieval recipe. After reviewing the problem setup ( § 3.1 ), we describe the changes that constitute BlockSearch ( § 3.2 ), our evaluation setup ( § 3.3 ), and the results ( § 3.4 ). These results motivate the later analysis of possible failure modes ( § 4 ) and promising lines for even further improvements ( § 5 ). 3.1 Setup Given a corpus of N N documents and a query, the model must generate the identifier of the document that best answers the query. The corpus is tokenized with at most T doc = 300 T_{\text{doc}}{=}300 tokens per document and prefilled into the KV cache; the query is appended, and the model autoregressively decodes a four-digit code in { 0 , … , 9999 } \{0,\dots,9999\} that maps back to one document (that’s hopefully relevant). This concretizes challenges C1 and C2 from § 1 : just 10,000 documents at ∼ \sim 100 tokens each well exceeds the 32K-token native context of the Qwen3-0.6B backbone, and the model must generalize to corpora substantially larger than those seen during training: again, a requirement that distinguishes retrievers from rerankers and has been largely overlooked in prior LM-retrieval work. 3.2 Method: BlockSearch We now describe BlockSearch : whenever possible, we follow prior ICR work, but our requirements C1 and C2 expose several limitations that motivate our proposed improvements. Prompt format. Prior in-context work assigns each document a sequential integer identifier from 1 1 to N N ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . In our regime, training-time IDs are a strict subset of inference IDs and risk overfitting to absolute position. We instead insert each document as <bos>Doc {code}: {text} (Doc {code})<eos> , with {code} drawn uniformly at random per training step, breaking any association between code, semantics, or position. We also drop the query prefix from prior work ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) : while it improves performance, it prevents corpus reuse across queries, which is cost-prohibitive at our scale. For a full example of a corpus/query prompt, we refer the reader to appendix A . Block-sparse attention. Causal prefill scales quadratically in tokens, which is prohibitive at our target N N . Since documents are disjoint, we use a block-sparse mask ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) : document tokens attend causally only within their own block, and the query block attends over the full corpus and causally to itself. Following common practice ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Gupta et al., 2025 ) , we reset RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) positions at each document start and shift the query to position 300. The mask is materialized via flex_attention ( Dong et al., 2024 ) . Training data. We train on the ReLabeled Hard Negatives (RLHN) version of BEIR ( Thakur et al., 2025 ) , which uses an LLM judge to prune false negatives from mined hard negatives in datasets such as MS MARCO ( Bajaj et al., 2016 ) . Per query we keep one pruned positive and 15 hard negatives; per-query relevance scores for the auxiliary loss are from Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . The training corpus totals ∼ \sim 100M tokens; full mix and cleaning details are in appendix C . Training regime. Inspired by in-batch contrastive training ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Qu et al., 2021 ) , we adapt in-batch negatives to this setting. For a batch of b b (query, 16-document) tuples (1 positive + 15 hard negatives each), we prefill all b × 16 b{\times}16 documents once (re-randomizing codes) and score every query against the shared corpus, converting one prefill into b b training signals. Every model is trained with 256 documents in its corpus, i.e. b = 16 b{=}16 . Training objective. We train with teacher forcing on the gold code, but this alon causes an exposure bias issue: at inference, each digit conditions on the model’s own potentially incorrect prefix, which lies off the training distribution. We therefore add an on-policy auxiliary loss. The model first rolls out a four-digit code from its own distribution with gradients disabled. For each digit position, we construct a teacher distribution from in-batch document scores, restricted to candidates whose prefix matches the rollout. We then replay the rollout with gradients enabled at the four answer positions and average the resulting cross-entropy losses. The total loss is ℒ = ℒ CE + λ ​ ℒ aux \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}} with λ \lambda ramped in after a warmup; the full algorithm can be found in algorithm 1 ( appendix F ). 3.3 Evaluation The model is judged by whether it can recover the relevant document from those placed in context; our metric is Recall@1 over the generated four-digit codes, decoded by a beam search over the digit sequence. Thus, these modifications extend functional LIMIT retrieval to larger corpora, rather than solving it, which remains an open problem. 7 Conclusion In this work, we presented the first systematic study of corpus-scale in-context retrieval with long-context language models, focusing on two requirements expected of practical retrieval systems: scaling to million-token corpora and generalizing to corpus sizes far beyond those seen during training. We showed that, with appropriate training and architectural modifications, LMs can perform meaningful retrieval far beyond their nominal training regime, approaching dense retrieval performance at moderate scales. The story is a tale of two cities: on benchmarks built around single-vector retrieval, our methods match a strong dense baseline at million-token scale, while on LIMIT, designed to defeat embedding similarity, they exceed it by nearly 3 × 3\times . At the same time, we identified attention dispersion as a fundamental scaling bottleneck: even when retrieval signals remain internally present, normalized attention mass collapses under extreme context growth. Motivated by this analysis, we demonstrated that length-aware tweaks to attention substantially improve retrieval performance at million-token scale. Together, our results suggest that scalable in-context retrieval is both promising and fundamentally constrained by attention dilution, motivating new directions for retrieval architectures and long-context modeling.
